newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU finance ministers meet on EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU finance ministers meet on EMU budget pact.

text.p: European Union finance ministers gathered on Monday to tackle differences over an accord that seeks to enforce budgetary rigour among countries forming a common currency.

While there is hope that a budget stability pact could be wrapped up in time for a December summit of EU leaders, finance ministers and monetary officials offered a mixed picture of how quickly an agreement might be reached.
"We will see whether it will happen this year," Johannes Ludewig, German economic state secretary told journalists ahead of the meeting.

Enforcing budgetary rigour within economic and monetary union (EMU) is a prime concern for nearly all of the EU's 15 nations, but nowhere is the objective greater than in Germany, a country wedded to sound monetary and budget policies.
Increasingly, German officials have become worried by what they perceive as a watering down of their initial proposal for the budget pact.
One of the main areas of concern is the lack of a precise definition of a severe economic downturn which would let governments running excessive deficits avoid sanctions.

Under the European Commission's draft plan, a government found to have an annual deficit above three percent of total output would have to put forward a credible plan within a specified period -- 10 months -- to correct it.

If they failed, the offending country would have to make an initial deposit with the EU, worth 0.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). For every percentage point above the three percent threshold, an added fine of 0.1 percent of GDP would be levied.

But if a country could demonstrate that its poor finances were due to an extraordinary economic downturn, it could presumably avoid any penalty. The Commission did not quantify the magnitude of a recession, but Germany very much wants to.
"I'm not sure whether we will reach agreement today," said Kenneth Clarke, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, adding that the discussion would focus on technical matters.
How much support Germany has is open to debate. Some suggested that the economic powerhouse was very much alone in its battle to secure a more stringent pact.

Asked whether he shared Germany's doubts over reaching an accord by year-end, Luxembourg's Finance Minister Jean Claude Juncker said he did not. He said such pessimism was largely confined to Germany.
The ministers will also assess recent progress on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism, linking the single currency to those not participating at the start of monetary union in 1999.
Should the ministers fail to make any headway over a budget pact at Monday's gathering, there will still be time to secure an accord when they meet next on December 2.
